analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' donations to national political parties and strengthens campaign disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 252-179 on August 6, 1998, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended, so the soft money ban never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop national political parties from raising or spending 'soft money' — unlimited contributions from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors that bypass normal contribution limits and disclosure. It would require state and local party committees to pay for federal election activity out of regulated, disclosed funds, and stop parties from routing money to tax-exempt groups to run issue ads. It would also speed up disclosure of who is paying for campaign ads and raise some individual contribution limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see untraceable special-interest money cut out of national party campaigns and get faster, searchable disclosure of who pays for political ads. Smaller donors benefit relatively, because the bill tightens the rules that let large donors give outside the normal limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want campaign money disclosed

how_it_helps.text: National party committees and their agents would be barred from soliciting, receiving, or spending any funds not subject to federal contribution limits and reporting requirements — the money known as soft money.

State, district, and local party committees would have to pay for federal election activity — voter registration drives, get-out-the-vote work, and ads naming federal candidates — only from regulated funds.
Party committees would be prohibited from soliciting funds for or donating to tax-exempt organizations, closing a route by which party money reached outside groups running issue ads.

Campaign reports would have to be filed electronically and posted on the Internet by the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and large independent expenditures late in a campaign would have to be reported within 24 to 48 hours.

The bill would prohibit fundraising on federal property, including the White House, require parties to reimburse the government for political use of Air Force One, and create criminal penalties for soliciting money in exchange for access to Air Force One, Marine One, or the Vice President's residence.
Penalties for knowing violations of campaign law would double, violations of the foreign-contribution ban would carry up to 10 years in prison, and contributions from minors would be banned.

analysis.who_pays: National and state political party committees, which lose unlimited soft money, and the large donors — corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals — who give it. Labor unions also lose under a provision letting nonmember employees opt out of paying for union political activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Political parties and large soft-money donors

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the aggregate limit on what one individual can give each year from $25,000 to $30,000 and creates a new $10,000 annual allowance per donor to state party committees, giving bigger donors more room rather than less.
The soft money ban exempts candidates who attend or speak at state party fundraising events in their home state, a carve-out that preserves a channel for large donations around candidates.

The bill codifies the Beck decision, requiring unions to reduce what nonmember employees pay in lieu of dues by the share spent on politics — organized labor opposed this as a cut to its political funds.

The bill defines 'express advocacy' narrowly, around phrases like 'vote for' or 'elect' and broadcast ads naming a candidate within 60 days of an election, leaving room for outside groups to run unregulated issue-advocacy ads that stop just short of telling anyone how to vote.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gain — shutting down unlimited, undisclosed party soft money — is real and large, and the faster disclosure would have made campaign money visible to any voter with an internet connection. But the bill is only a partial reform: it raises some individual limits in the same breath as banning soft money, exempts candidate appearances at state party fundraisers, and its narrow definition of express advocacy leaves outside-group issue ads largely untouched. An honest supporter would call it the achievable version of reform, not the whole thing.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 252-179 in August 1998, but the Senate put it on its calendar and never brought it to a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Rep. Asa Hutchinson introduced the bill on July 17, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Oversight.
It drew 78 cosponsors — 51 Democrats and 27 Republicans — unusual bipartisan support for a campaign finance bill.
The House debated it intermittently from May through August 1998 under structured rules, with dozens of amendment votes; a substitute offered by Rep. Shays became the bill's operative text.
On August 6, 1998, the House passed the bill 252-179, with Democrats voting 190-15 in favor and Republicans 61-164 against.
The Senate received the bill on August 31, 1998, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on September 9 — but no floor vote ever occurred.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the bill died with the Congress, and unlimited soft money remained legal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who fund them came out ahead: with no Senate vote, the soft money system stayed intact and kept growing through the 2000 election, until a successor law finally passed in 2002.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Party soft-money operations and their big donors

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split mostly by party: Democrats backed it 190-15 while Republicans opposed it 164-61, though a third of House Republicans crossed over to pass it 252-179.

industries.note: The bill cuts off the parties' unlimited soft money pipeline but partially compensates with higher hard-money limits and a $10,000 state committee allowance per donor. Party committees fought soft money bans precisely because soft money funded their federal election operations outside any limits.

Large corporations and unions would lose the ability to give six- and seven-figure undisclosed donations to national parties. Their interest in avoiding disclosure and limits runs against voters' interest in knowing who pays for campaigns.

Beyond the soft money rules, the bill codifies the Beck decision, requiring unions to let nonmember employees opt out of paying for union political activity and to explain the reduction. Unions see this as draining their political funds; its benefit to individual nonmember workers depends on whether they object to the political spending.

Candidates who pledge to cap their own spending at $50,000 get a certification that shields them from unlimited party coordinated spending by opponents; candidates who spend freely lose that protection, and party coordinated-spending limits no longer apply against them. The provision pushes million-dollar self-funders toward disclosure but does not stop them.
